clue.text: Instrument, Gallic warning device

blocks.note: Gallic means from France
a car's horn warns other road users

explanation.surface: A list entry: an instrument, then a French alarm or siren.
explanation.definitionFit: This brass instrument with a coiled tube is a standard member of the orchestra, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Foreign Office caught out over American target

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for the British Foreign Office
in cricket scoring, c stands for a batsman caught out
US is short for United States, hence American

explanation.surface: A diplomatic blunder: the Foreign Office is caught out with an American target.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' places the first pieces above the last; it simply joins them here.
explanation.definitionFit: A focus is the central point that attention is aimed at, a synonym of target.

clue.text: Competitor in event ran third

indicators.note: the answer is said to be inside the next words, so read straight through them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A sports report: a competitor in some race finished third.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrant is someone who has entered a contest, so a synonym for a competitor.

clue.text: Cuts of meat in the refrigerator?

definitions.text: Cuts of meat in the refrigerator?

blocks.clueFragment: Cuts of meat in the refrigerator?
blocks.note: surface reading: joints of meat being chilled
setter's reading: cuts are snubs, deliberate ignorings of someone, and the phrase for those also describes chilled joints

explanation.walkthrough: To cut someone is to snub them; the answer is the idiom for snubs, and taken literally it is chilled shoulder joints.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means deliberate unfriendliness, which is what a social cut is; literally it is refrigerated shoulder meat.

clue.text: Members of a ship's crew losing easily

blocks.note: sailors are called hands
a team that is down is behind, losing

explanation.surface: Sailors losing a contest with little trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'easily' describe the losing, but it is the definition and the sense flips to winning.
explanation.definitionFit: To win by this idiom is to win effortlessly, so it means with ease.

clue.text: Drill found in boulevard, and a little bit of money

indicators.note: one thing found in another is held within it

blocks.note: rue is French for a street
physical exercise drill, as school PE

explanation.surface: Someone drilling in a street turns up a few coins.
explanation.definitionFit: The rupee is the currency unit of India and Pakistan, a modest unit of money.

clue.text: Blow the whistle on store

blocks.note: first meaning: inform on someone to the authorities
second meaning: a retail premises

explanation.surface: An informer exposing a store's wrongdoing.
explanation.definitionFit: To shop someone is British slang for betraying them to the police; a shop is also a place selling goods.

clue.text: Having blown top, this Conservative in the past

indicators.note: losing the top of a word in a down clue means its first letter goes

blocks.note: the word with its opening letter removed
a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A Conservative who lost his temper is now finished politically.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is history means it is over and gone, belonging to the past.

clue.text: Measure of cloth put inside appropriate mechanical device

indicators.note: one item is placed within the other

blocks.note: proper means fitting
an ell is an old length used for cloth, about 45 inches

explanation.surface: Fabric being measured and fitted into a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw on a ship or plane is a mechanical device that drives it forward, so an example of the class.

clue.text: Language of malicious woman in front of boy

blocks.note: a spiteful woman is called a cat
any boy's name will do

explanation.surface: A spiteful woman speaking ahead of a young lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in front of' just places the first piece before the second.
explanation.definitionFit: This Romance tongue is spoken in Catalonia and Andorra, so it is an example of a language.

clue.text: Constable I included as very good artist

indicators.note: something included is taken in, enclosed by the word around it

blocks.note: Police Constable
taken as written
taken as written
so means very, as in so good

explanation.surface: An art claim: I rank with Constable as a very good painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Constable the painter is the misdirection; it is a police officer, and 'very good' must be split.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish painter who co-founded Cubism is among the most celebrated artists of the 20th century.

clue.text: Empty the packs and prepare for action

blocks.note: first meaning, literal: take the packs of cards off the table
second meaning: the naval order to make a ship ready for battle

explanation.surface: Unloading kit bags before going into battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Packs are packs of cards, decks; the phrase comes from clearing a warship's decks before a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means getting ready for a task by removing obstacles; literally it removes card decks.

clue.text: Poles thinly dispersed, for the most part

indicators.note: only most of the word is kept, so its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: sparse means thinly scattered

explanation.surface: A population of Polish people spread thinly over a region.
explanation.walkthrough: Poles looks like the nationality; it means long wooden poles.
explanation.definitionFit: Spars are the stout poles used as masts and booms on a ship.

clue.text: Docker's severed toe finally amputated, unfortunately

indicators.note: the end letter is cut off the word just before
things going unfortunately go wrong, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
the word without its final letter

explanation.surface: A dockyard accident: a worker's crushed toe had to be removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docker's' is the definition plus 'is'; only the toe loses its last letter before the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A stevedore loads and unloads ships, the same job as a docker.

clue.text: Early star or moon excited Halley, say

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so the letters are agitated into a new order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters are the fodder

explanation.surface: Halley's excitement at a morning star or the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: Edmond Halley, of the comet, held the official post of royal astronomer in Britain from 1720.
explanation.definitionFit: Halley was the second holder of this British title, so he is an example of it.

clue.text: Nervously sat with an able actor

indicators.note: a nervous person fidgets, so the letters shift about restlessly

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone waiting anxiously beside a talented performer.
explanation.definitionFit: He was an English stage and screen actor, star of Women in Love and The Go-Between.

clue.text: Ivy, perhaps, always growing

blocks.note: ever means always, as in ever hopeful
green describes living, growing plants

explanation.surface: Ivy that never stops spreading.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy keeps its leaves all year, so it is an example of a plant that stays leafy through winter.

clue.text: Working lunches with a macabre lawyer

indicators.note: working material is being processed and changed, so the letters are remade

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Business lunches with a ghoulish solicitor.
explanation.definitionFit: A derogatory term for a lawyer who touts for accident victims' compensation claims, so an example of a lawyer.

clue.text: Resilient youth, reportedly leading worker

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: a youth is a boy, which is said like a floating marker
the worker ant is the crossword's usual worker

explanation.surface: A tough young man reported to be heading the workforce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading' puts the first piece before the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Buoyant means able to float, and figuratively cheerful and quick to recover, which is resilient.

clue.text: Top expert on a Malibu board?

blocks.note: riding waves on a board off the Californian beach
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: A champion of the Californian surf.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are taken in answer order: what you do on the board, then the expert.
explanation.definitionFit: The surface is the uppermost layer of something, its top.

clue.text: The missile to backfire?

blocks.note: first meaning: the curved Aboriginal throwing stick that returns to the thrower
second meaning, a verb: to rebound on the person responsible

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a question about whether a missile will fail; the noun and the verb are the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The thrown stick comes back, so the word also means a plan that returns to harm its maker.

clue.text: Greek starter?

blocks.note: surface reading: a first course in a Greek restaurant, such as meze
setter's reading: the first of the twenty-four Greek letters

explanation.walkthrough: Starter suggests food; it is the first letter in the Greek script.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the first of the Greek letters, so it literally starts off the sequence.

clue.text: Cook nearly all staple food Greek-style

indicators.note: nearly all of a word keeps everything but its last letter

blocks.note: to do food is to cook it, as in do the vegetables
rice, the staple, cut short

explanation.surface: Cooking a staple food the way the Greeks do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' looks like an anagram signal but is a verb giving two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Doric is one of the classical Greek architectural orders, and also an ancient Greek dialect, hence in Greek style.

clue.text: Chapter on English pianist making musical

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for chapter
Dame Myra Hess, the English pianist famed for her wartime National Gallery concerts

explanation.surface: A book chapter on a pianist who wrote a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is the 1984 musical by Tim Rice with ABBA's Benny and Björn, so it is an example of a musical.

clue.text: Pulls to pieces product of Pasteur

indicators.note: a product is made out of raw material, so the letters are manufactured into something new

blocks.note: the French scientist's name supplies the letters

explanation.surface: Someone tearing apart a product of the scientist Louis Pasteur.
explanation.definitionFit: To rip something into shreds is to destroy it entirely, and the phrasal verb is a synonym for that.

clue.text: Enclosed area for 150 in eastern part of church

indicators.note: one item placed in another sits within it

blocks.note: E is short for east
the nave is the main body of a church
CL is 150 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Room for a congregation of 150 at the east end of a church.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclave is a territory wholly surrounded by another, so an enclosed region.

clue.text: Building area? Eyesore, from what one hears

indicators.note: this concerns what reaches the ear, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: something ugly is called a sight, as in you look a sight

explanation.surface: Gossip that a building plot is an eyesore.
explanation.definitionFit: A building site is the area where construction happens, so the word names such a plot.

clue.text: Nastiness surprisingly involving a French composer

indicators.note: a surprising result is unexpected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, and folded into the mix

explanation.surface: A French composer caught up in some unexpected unpleasantness.
explanation.definitionFit: Camille Saint-Saëns wrote The Carnival of the Animals and was a leading French composer.
